But  my  mother  was  very  ill  all  her  life.  She  used  to  have  fainting  fits  in  the  street,  and

had  a stroke  in  1959.  It  never  seemed  easy  for  me  to  talk  with  her,  and  she  never  volunteered 
much  information.  But  I recal  that  she  used  to  hold  court  in  the  kitchen,  as  my  sister  and  I 
called  it.  Many  people,  usually  women,  came  to  the  house  for  advice.  Divorces  and  other 
problems  were  discussed  in  secret  upstairs,  away  from  my  father  and  the  children.  There  also 
seemed  to  be  sessions  of  fortune  telling  with  cards.  It  was  all  vaguely  connected  with  her 
Romanian  past. 

Around  1965,  just  before  I got  married,  Martha,  now  my  wife,  came  back  from  Saint  Louis 
with  me  to  New  York  because  my  father  was  ill.  He  was  in  hospital  with  a bad  hernia.  Martha 
gave  blood  on  his  behalf.  We  went  to  visit  him  in  Maimonides  Hospital.  My  mother  was  sitting 
next  to  the  bed,  her  cane  leaning  against  the  chair.  She  wore  leg  braces  to  help  her  walk.  Her 
face  was  still  distorted  from  the  stroke.  When  Martha  and  I entered,  she  wept  and  kissed  us 
both.  My  father  smiled  from  his  bed.  He  looked  weak  and  tired,  but  the  doctors  said  the  danger 
was  passed.  As  we  chatted  quietly,  an  old  man  in  the  next  bed  began  to  motion  to  me.  My 
mother  said  to  him,  that  yes  I was  the  son,  and  the  old  man  - he  was  short  and  wizened, 
practically  not  there  at  all  - started  to  climb  out  of  the  bed.  He  kept  mumbling  things  I could 
not  understand.  My  mother  said  that  he  knew  who  I was,  the  descendant  of  the  grand  rabbi, 
the  inheritor  to  the  throne  of  David.  The  old  man  was  kneeling  at  my  feet.  It  was  very 
embarrasing,  and  I said  something  about  not  wanting  such  a gesture,  and  I left  the  room. 
Later,  when  I came  back,  the  old  man  was  gone,  and  my  mother  said  the  nurses  had  taken 
him  away  for  a bath.  That  was,  in  all  its  strangeness,  the  closest  I ever  came  to  knowing 
anything  about  my  grandfather. 

Now,  there  are  a few  relatives  in  America  I occasionally  see,  but  they  are  on  my  father's 
side,  the  ones  who  came  from  Poland  and  Ukraine,  hence  my  original  name.  My  father 
changed  Simnowith  to  Simms,  and  his  father  had  changed  it  from  Djimnaboufski.  It  is  sad, 
disappointing,  and  shameful  that  all  that  history  that  remains  to  be  known  is  lost,  and  I have 
almost  nothing  to  pass  on  to  my  own  children,  David,  who  is  a farmer  od  New  Zealand,  and 
Meliors,  with  her  daughter,  who  live  in  upstate  New  York.

FRAGMENTS  OF  MEMORY 

THE  GRAND  RABBI  OF  DOROHOI 

By  NORMAN  SIMMS 

There  is  so  little  information,  and  there  is  no  one  left  to  ask.  My  sister,  who  is  younger 
than  I by  seven  years,  has  no  memory  even  of  what  little  I know.  For  whatever  reasons,  my 
mother,  who  died  in  1969,  only  told  me  a little.  Between  her  illness  and  my  own  childish 
indifference,  the  time  for  learning  about  our  past  is  now  gone.  When  I received  the  first  book 
from  the  Society  of  Descendents  of  Dorohoi,  I wept,  and  felt  a deep  guilt  sweep  over  me:  that 
so  much  of  history  should  have  come  to  this,  a fifty-three  year  old  man  who  has  forgotten  his 
family's  past. 

But  I have  a few  fragments  of  memory  about  the  family's  history  on  my  mother's  side,  the 
part  who  came  from  Dorohoi.  The  name  of  the  town  and  the  Romanian  background  is  clear, 
but  my  grandmother's  name  is  not.  She  married  twice,  once  to  a Goldman,  and  then  to  a 
Hermann,  and  I cannot  be  sure  that  her  maiden  name  was  Wilowitz. 

The  history  that  remains  goes  like  this. 

My  grandmother  was  Molly  (Malka),  and  her  father  was  the  grand  rabbi  in  Dorohoi.  In  the 
late  nineteenth  century  he  claimed  that  he  was  a direct  descendant  of  King  David.  There  were 
pamphlet  debates.  He  Is  said  to  have  won.  The  family  owned  some  land  and  were  respected. 
Early  In  this  century  - I keep  guessing  it  was  around  1 909,  the  time  of  the  Peasants'  Revolt  - 
Molly  was  sixteen.  She  was  making  the  grand  tour  with  a governess,  visiting  distant  members 
of  the  family.  In  Philadelphia  she  received  a telegram.  It  said  briefly:  Do  not  return.  The 
family  have  been  killed  in  a pogrom.  So  she  stayed  in  America.  My  mother  claimed  that  the 
relatives  in  Philadelphia  took  advantage  of  this  innocent  young  girl,  this  greenhorn,  and  cheated 
her  out  of  her  fortune,  land  that  was  owned  in  New  York  and  elsewhere.  The  memory  is 
unclear. 

Soon  after,  I was  told.  Grandma  Molly  married  her  first  husband,  a man  named  Goldner 
and  she  had  a son,  Jack.  I met  him  several  times  as  a child.  He  had  a daughter,  my  cousin 
Bernice.  Jack  was  interested  in  radios  and  later  sold  leather  jackets  in  Denver.  He  died  in 
California  about  fifteen  years  ago. 

When  Mr.  Goldner  died,  my  grandmother  re-married  Moses  (Moe)  Hermann,  who  was 
himself  a widower  with  a son,  Bertram.  Bertram  was  a sailor  and  disappeared  early  in  the 
1940s.  I recall  my  mother  writing  letters  to  the  War  Department  In  Washington  to  try  to  find 
out  what  happened  to  him.  She  never  did.  There  is  a vague  memory  that  he  had  sent  a 
postcard  from  Hawaii  just  before  the  attack  on  Pearl  Harbour. 

Moe  was  a cloth  cutter  and  when  my  father  went  Into  the  army  In  1943,  he  made  me  a
